numberItems.stem: How far ahead do most good drivers look?
options: About 100 feet ahead
At least 12 to 15 seconds ahead
About 200 feet ahead
numberItems.explanation: Most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, the distance you will travel in that time (p. 2-12).

numberItems.stem: You are driving at lower (city) speeds. Looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead means looking about:
options: One block ahead
A quarter of a mile ahead
500 feet ahead
numberItems.explanation: At lower speeds, 12 to 15 seconds is about one block; at highway speeds it is about a quarter of a mile (p. 2-12).

numberItems.stem: You are on the open highway. How far ahead should you be looking to cover 12 to 15 seconds?
options: About one block
About 200 feet
About a quarter of a mile
numberItems.explanation: At highway speeds, 12 to 15 seconds ahead is about a quarter of a mile (p. 2-12, Figure 2.6).

numberItems.stem: When you look ahead, what 2 main things should you look for?
options: Traffic and road conditions
Your mirrors and your gauges
Horn signals and headlight flashes
numberItems.explanation: Look ahead for traffic (vehicles entering, turning, brake lights) and road conditions (hills, curves, signals and signs) (pp. 2-12 to 2-13).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Under CVC §26709, how many mirrors must every California-registered motor vehicle have, at minimum?
options: At least 1, on the left side
At least 2, including 1 on the left side
At least 2, including 1 on the right side
numberItems.explanation: Every California-registered motor vehicle must have at least 2 mirrors, including 1 on the left-hand side (p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Your required mirrors must give a clear view of the roadway to the rear for a distance of at least:
options: 100 feet
500 feet
200 feet
numberItems.explanation: The mirrors must give a clear view to the rear for at least 200 feet (CVC §26709, p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: Compared with a flat mirror, a convex ("fisheye") mirror shows a wider area, but things in it look:
options: Smaller and farther away than they really are
Larger and closer than they really are
The same size, in a narrower view
numberItems.explanation: Everything appears smaller in a convex mirror and seems farther away than it really is (p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: When can mirror adjustment be checked accurately?
options: While driving at highway speed
Before a trip, with the trailer(s) straight
With the trailer at an angle so its side shows
numberItems.explanation: Check mirror adjustment before the start of any trip; it can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight (p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: During a lane change, how many times should you check your mirrors?
options: Once, just before you move over
3 times: before, during and after
4 times: before, after signaling, right after starting, and after finishing
numberItems.explanation: Check your mirrors before the lane change, after signaling, right after starting the change, and after completing it (p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: Which 4 special situations require more than regular mirror checks?
options: Lane changes, turns, merges and tight maneuvers
Night driving, rain, fog and snow
Starting, stopping, parking and idling
numberItems.explanation: The special situations are lane changes, turns, merges and tight maneuvers (p. 2-13).

numberItems.stem: What are the handbook's 3 good rules for using turn signals?
options: Signal early, cancel the signal as you start turning, and flash your brake lights
Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal after the turn
Signal only when other vehicles are near, and cancel before the turn
numberItems.explanation: The 3 rules: signal early, signal continuously (don't cancel until the turn is complete), and cancel your signal after the turn (p. 2-14).

numberItems.stem: What is the best way to keep other drivers from trying to pass you when you turn?
options: Tap your horn as you begin the turn
Signal early, well before you turn
Swing wide to the left before turning right
numberItems.explanation: Signal well before you turn; it is the best way to keep others from trying to pass you (p. 2-14).

numberItems.stem: You see you will need to slow down. How should you warn the drivers behind you?
options: Wave them around with your arm
Turn on your right turn signal
Tap the brake pedal lightly a few times so the brake lights flash
numberItems.explanation: A few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, should warn following drivers (p. 2-14).

numberItems.stem: You must stop on the shoulder of a road. Within how long must you put out your emergency warning devices?
options: Within 10 minutes
Within 15 minutes
Within 30 minutes
numberItems.explanation: If you stop on a road or its shoulder, you must put out emergency warning devices within 10 minutes (p. 2-14).

numberItems.stem: You stop beside a **one-way** highway. Where do the three warning devices go?
options: Within 10 ft of a corner, 100 ft behind and 100 ft ahead
100 ft, 200 ft and 500 ft behind the vehicle
10 ft, 100 ft and 200 ft toward approaching traffic
numberItems.explanation: On a one-way or divided highway, place warning devices 10, 100 and 200 feet toward approaching traffic (p. 2-14, Figure 2.8).

numberItems.stem: You stop on a two-lane road with traffic in both directions. Where does the warning device in front of your vehicle go?
options: About 100 feet ahead of the vehicle
About 200 feet ahead of the vehicle
None goes ahead; all three go behind
numberItems.explanation: On a two-lane or undivided road: one within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, one 100 feet behind and one 100 feet ahead (p. 2-15, Figure 2.9).

numberItems.stem: You must move the rearmost triangle back beyond a hill or curve if it keeps other drivers from seeing your vehicle within:
options: 100 feet
500 feet
200 feet
numberItems.explanation: Go back beyond any hill, curve or obstruction that prevents drivers from seeing the vehicle within 500 feet (p. 2-15, Figure 2.10).
